title: Learning safely
subject: Digital safety
description: Learn how to study with a safe nickname and protect private information on shared devices.
content: A safe learning app should help children learn without asking for real names, document numbers, addresses, phone numbers, family details, or photos of private documents. Learners can use nicknames. If an app, website, or person asks for private information, stop and ask a trusted adult first.
goal: Use LearnBridge safely on a shared device without sharing private personal information.
steps: Look at the learner nickname box. Choose a short nickname, not a real full name.
Read these private examples together: phone number, exact location, ID document, family situation, and private photo.
Sort each example as safe for learning or private to protect.
Practice saying: I do not want to share that. I will ask my teacher.
Use the app without entering real names, documents, or location details.
practice: Make two columns on paper: OK for learning and Keep private. Put these words in the right column: nickname, favorite color, phone number, real full name, lesson progress, exact address, document photo.
checkQuestion: Which is safer to type in this app: a nickname or a real full name? Why?
teacherNote: Keep this lesson calm and practical. Do not ask children to reveal examples from their own family. UNICEF child online protection guidance emphasizes protecting children's identity and personal information online.

references.title: UNICEF: Online safety and data protection

title: Number practice
subject: Math
description: Build early number confidence by counting, grouping, comparing, and explaining with real objects.
content: Numbers are easier to understand when learners can touch, move, and group real objects. This lesson uses safe nearby objects so children can count aloud, compare groups, and explain what they notice.
goal: Count objects from 1 to 10, compare two groups, and explain which group has more or fewer.
steps: Warm up by counting fingers from 1 to 10 together.
Place 5 safe objects in a row. Touch each object once while counting aloud.
Move the objects into two groups, such as 2 and 3. Count each group.
Ask: Which group has more? Which group has fewer? How do you know?
Add one more object and count again. Then remove one object and count again.
practice: Use pencils, stones, leaves, cups, or paper pieces. Learners work in pairs: one learner makes a group, the other counts and says whether the group has more, fewer, or the same number as another group.
checkQuestion: Show 7 objects. Split them into two groups. How many are in each group?
teacherNote: Use concrete objects and let learners explain with words, pointing, or drawing. Khan Academy Kids and Global Digital Library both emphasize early math practice through accessible, child-friendly activities.

references.title: Global Digital Library: early math and reading resources
Khan Academy Kids: early math and reading app

title: Thai daily words
subject: Thai language
description: Practice a small set of Thai words that can help learners greet people and ask for basic help.
content: Thai words can help learners move through daily life more safely, especially when asking for water, toilets, school, hospital, or help. Pronunciation can vary, so a local Thai speaker should review this lesson before real use.
goal: Recognize and practice simple Thai words for greetings, basic needs, and asking for help.
steps: Listen first. The teacher says each word slowly: sawatdee, khop khun, nam, hong nam, chuai duai, rong rian, rong phayaban.
Repeat as a group. Do not force learners to speak alone if they are shy.
Match each word to a meaning: hello, thank you, water, toilet, help, school, hospital.
Practice pointing or showing a card if speaking feels hard.
Practice one useful phrase: chuai duai, which means help me or please help.
practice: The teacher gives a situation: I need water, I need the toilet, I need help, I need school, or I need hospital. Learners choose the useful word by speaking, pointing, or holding up a card.
checkQuestion: Which Thai word or phrase could you use if you need help?
teacherNote: Ask a local Thai speaker to review pronunciation and wording. This lesson is for basic survival communication, not formal Thai language instruction.

title: Reading practice
subject: Literacy
description: Practice reading short sentences, pointing to words, and changing one word to make meaning.
content: Reading grows through small repeated practice. In this lesson, learners read a short sentence, point to each word, copy it if paper is available, and change one word to make a new sentence.
goal: Read a short sentence with support, identify words, and change one word to create a new sentence.
steps: Teacher reads first: I can learn today.
Learners read together slowly three times.
Point to each word while reading: I / can / learn / today.
Ask: Which word tells what we do? Which word tells when?
Change one word to make a new sentence, such as: I can count today, I can read today, or We can learn today.
practice: Learners work with a partner. One reads the sentence. One points to the words. Then they choose one word to change and read the new sentence together.
checkQuestion: Read your new sentence. Which word did you change?
teacherNote: Use shared reading before individual reading. Global Digital Library focuses on accessible early grade reading resources in languages children use and understand.

references.title: Global Digital Library: early reading resources
UNESCO: Global Digital Library and early reading

title: English greetings
subject: English
description: Practice simple English greetings for meeting teachers, helpers, and classmates.
content: Practice these greetings: Hello. My name is ___. Thank you. Please help me. Say each phrase slowly. Then practice with a partner using a safe nickname instead of a real full name.
goal: Practice simple English phrases for greetings and asking for help.
realLifeUse: Use these phrases when arriving at a class, meeting a new person, thanking someone, or asking a teacher or worker for help.

vocabulary.meaning: a greeting used when you meet someone
a polite word used when asking

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Hello. My name is Lin. What is your name?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: My name is May. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Nice to meet you too.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Please help me find the classroom.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Yes. It is this way.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Thank you for your help.

steps: Say together: Hello.
Say together: My name is ___. Use a safe nickname.
Say together: Thank you.
Say together: Please help me.
Practice a short greeting with a partner.
practice: Learners practice a two-line conversation: Hello. My name is ___. Hello. Please help me. They can use safe nicknames only.

exercises.question: What is the best phrase when meeting someone for the first time?
exercises.explanation: 'Nice to meet you' is a polite response during a first introduction.

exercises.question: Choose the polite request.
exercises.explanation: Adding 'please' makes the request polite and natural.

exercises.question: What can you say after someone helps you?
exercises.explanation: Use 'Thank you for your help' to show appreciation.

finalTask: Imagine it is your first day in a new class. Greet one person, introduce yourself with a nickname, ask for help finding the classroom, and thank them. Practice until you can say all four parts without reading.
takeaway: Begin with 'Hello.'
Use 'Nice to meet you' during a first introduction.
Use 'Please help me' for a polite request.
Thank the person after receiving help.
checkQuestion: What English phrase can you use when you need help?
teacherNote: Let learners practice in pairs after group repetition. Remind them that nicknames are enough for learning activities.

title: Introduce yourself
subject: English
description: Build a short introduction using a name, where you are from, and one interest.
content: A simple introduction helps people begin a conversation at school, work, or in a new community. Use a nickname when you do not need to share your legal name.
goal: Say and understand a simple three-sentence personal introduction.
realLifeUse: Use this skill when meeting a classmate, joining a course, speaking to a volunteer, or beginning a job interview.

vocabulary.meaning: the place where you began or grew up
to have your home in a place
to use a language when talking
wanting to learn or know more about something

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Hello. My name is Maya. What is your name?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Hi, Maya. I am Ko. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Nice to meet you too. Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I am from Myanmar, and I live in Thailand now.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What are you interested in?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I am interested in computers and English.

steps: Read aloud: Hello. My name is Maya.
Add a place: I am from Myanmar.
Add one interest: I like music.
Join the sentences: Hello. My name is Maya. I am from Myanmar. I like music.
Ask a partner: What is your name? What do you like?
practice: Choose a nickname, a country or town, and one interest. Say your introduction twice. On the second try, look up from the screen and speak from memory.

exercises.question: Which sentence tells someone your current home?
exercises.explanation: Use 'I live in ...' for the place where your home is now.

exercises.question: Choose the best reply to: What are you interested in?
exercises.explanation: 'I am interested in ...' introduces a subject or activity you want to learn more about.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence: I ___ Burmese and English.
exercises.explanation: We use 'speak' before the name of a language.

finalTask: Imagine you are joining a new class. Prepare a five-sentence introduction using your name or nickname, where you are from, where you live now, the languages you speak, and one interest. Say it aloud without reading every word. Then ask another person two questions: What is your name? What are you interested in?
takeaway: Use 'I am from ...' for your place of origin.
Use 'I live in ...' for your current home.
Use 'I speak ...' for languages.
Use 'I am interested in ...' for interests or learning goals.
checkQuestion: Can you introduce yourself using three short sentences?
teacherNote: Model the introduction first. Learners may replace the place sentence with 'I live in ___' or skip it if they prefer not to share that information.

title: Ask when you do not understand
subject: English
description: Practice useful questions for lessons, instructions, and everyday conversations.
content: Asking a clear question is a learning skill. These short phrases help when someone speaks too quickly or an instruction is unclear.
goal: Use four polite phrases to ask for repetition, meaning, or help.
realLifeUse: Use these questions in a classroom, workplace, clinic, shop, or public office when instructions are unclear.

vocabulary.meaning: to know the meaning of something
to say or do something again
at a speed that is easier to follow
to have a particular definition or message

patterns: Could you say that again, please?
Could you speak more slowly, please?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Please submit the form before noon.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: I do not understand. What does submit mean?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: It means give the completed form to me.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Could you say the time again, please?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Before twelve o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Thank you. I understand now.

steps: Say: I do not understand.
Say: Please say that again.
Say: Please speak slowly.
Ask: What does this mean?
Practice choosing the best phrase for a fast speaker, a new word, and a difficult instruction.
practice: Partner A reads a short instruction quickly. Partner B asks them to repeat or speak slowly. Switch roles, then use 'What does this mean?' for one unfamiliar word.

exercises.question: Someone speaks too fast. What should you ask?
options: Could you speak more slowly, please?
exercises.explanation: Ask the speaker to slow down when speed is the problem.

exercises.question: You hear an unfamiliar word. Which question is most useful?
exercises.explanation: Ask what a word means when you need its definition.

exercises.question: Which request is the most polite?
options: Could you say that again, please?
exercises.explanation: 'Could you ... please?' is a polite request pattern.

finalTask: Ask another person to give you a two-step instruction. Use at least two clarification phrases before repeating the instruction back in your own words. Finish with: I understand now. Thank you.
takeaway: Say clearly when you do not understand.
Ask for repetition when you missed the message.
Ask for slower speech when speed is the problem.
Ask what a word means when vocabulary is the problem.
checkQuestion: What can you say when someone is speaking too quickly?
teacherNote: Treat asking questions as a positive skill. Allow learners to read the phrases from the screen until they become comfortable.

title: Signs and simple directions
subject: English
description: Recognize common signs and follow short directions in schools, stations, clinics, and public places.
content: A few common words can make public places easier to understand. Focus on meaning first, then practice giving and following one-step directions.
goal: Recognize six common signs and follow four basic direction words.
realLifeUse: Use this skill to find entrances, exits, toilets, information desks, clinics, and transport stops.

vocabulary.meaning: the place where you go into a building
the place where you leave a building
a place where you can ask questions
the two directions on either side of you

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Excuse me. Where is the information desk?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Go straight and turn right.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is it next to the entrance?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Yes. It is across from the ticket office.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: You're welcome.

steps: Read the signs: Entrance, Exit, Toilet, Information, Hospital, and Bus stop.
Practice the directions: left, right, straight, and stop.
Say: Go straight. Turn left. Turn right. Stop here.
Draw a simple map with a start point and one destination.
Guide a partner across the map using two or three short directions.
practice: Place three paper labels around the room, such as Exit, Information, and Bus stop. One learner asks, 'Where is the bus stop?' Another gives a simple direction using left, right, or straight.

exercises.question: Which sign shows the way out of a building?
exercises.explanation: An exit is the place where you leave a building.

exercises.question: Which question asks for a location?
exercises.explanation: Use 'Where is ...?' to ask for the location of a place.

exercises.question: What does 'go straight' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Go straight' means continue forward without turning left or right.

finalTask: Draw a small map containing an entrance, information desk, toilet, and bus stop. Ask a partner for one location, then guide them with at least three direction phrases. Switch roles and try a new destination.
takeaway: Use 'Where is ...?' to ask for a place.
Use straight, left, and right to guide movement.
Use next to and across from to describe a location.
Repeat the direction back if you are unsure.
checkQuestion: Which sign shows where you can ask for help or directions?
teacherNote: Use signs learners are likely to see locally. Explain that real signs may use symbols or another language as well as English.

title: English foundations checkpoint
subject: English
description: Combine greetings, introductions, clarification questions, signs, and directions in one practical challenge.
content: This checkpoint brings the four English lessons together. Review any lesson you need, then complete the questions and the real-world scenario.
goal: Use the English foundations skills together in a realistic first-day situation.
realLifeUse: Use this combined skill when arriving at a new school, training centre, workplace, clinic, or community service.
patterns: I am from ___, and I live in ___.
Could you say that again, please?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Hello. My name is Zaw. I am here for the computer class.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: Welcome. Please register at the information desk.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: What does register mean?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: Write your name on the class list.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: I understand. Where is the information desk?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: Go straight. It is next to the classroom.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Thank you for your help.

steps: Read the conversation once for meaning.
Read it again and identify the greeting, introduction, clarification question, and direction.
Replace the learner's name and class with your own example.
Practice the conversation aloud, then switch roles.
Complete the quick check before doing the final scenario.

exercises.question: Which sentence is an introduction?
exercises.explanation: 'My name is ...' introduces you to another person.

exercises.question: You do not know the word register. What should you ask?
exercises.explanation: Use 'What does ... mean?' for an unfamiliar word.

exercises.question: Which question helps you find a classroom?
exercises.explanation: Use 'Where is ...?' to ask for a location.

exercises.question: What should you say after receiving directions?
exercises.explanation: Thank the person after they help you.

finalTask: Role-play arriving at a new class. Greet the staff member, introduce yourself, explain which class you need, ask the meaning of one unfamiliar word, ask where the classroom is, repeat the direction, and thank them. Complete the scenario without reading every sentence.
takeaway: You can begin a conversation politely.
You can give a short introduction.
You can ask when you do not understand.
You can ask for and follow simple directions.
checkQuestion: Can you complete the arrival scenario using at least five English sentences?
teacherNote: Observe whether learners can communicate meaning rather than requiring perfect grammar or pronunciation. Let them review earlier lessons before retrying.

title: Japanese first phrases
subject: Japanese
description: Practice polite Japanese phrases for greeting someone, asking for attention, and saying that you do not understand.
content: Practical Japanese starts with short expressions you can use in real situations. Listen to a trusted pronunciation source when internet is available, then keep the lesson and audio on your device for offline practice.
goal: Recognize and use five polite phrases in a simple daily conversation.
steps: おはようございます (ohayou gozaimasu) — Good morning.
すみません (sumimasen) — Excuse me / I am sorry.
わかりません (wakarimasen) — I do not understand.
もういちど おねがいします (mou ichido onegaishimasu) — Please say it again.
ありがとうございます (arigatou gozaimasu) — Thank you.
practice: Choose one situation: meeting a teacher, asking a station worker for attention, or not understanding an instruction. Practice a two-line conversation using two phrases. Repeat after reliable audio when available.
checkQuestion: Which phrase can you use when you need someone to repeat an instruction?
teacherNote: Prioritize listening and speaking before writing systems. Use Japan Foundation audio for pronunciation and avoid presenting romanization as a complete substitute for learning Japanese script.

references.title: Irodori Starter: Japanese for Life in Japan

title: Calm breathing
subject: Wellbeing
description: A short calming activity for stressful learning days.
content: Sit comfortably if you can. Breathe in slowly while counting 1, 2, 3. Breathe out slowly while counting 1, 2, 3. Repeat five times. Notice one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, and one thing you can feel.
goal: Practice a short calming routine for stressful moments.
steps: Sit or stand in a comfortable position if you can.
Breathe in slowly while counting 1, 2, 3.
Breathe out slowly while counting 1, 2, 3.
Repeat five times.
Notice one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, and one thing you can feel.
practice: Do the breathing routine together for one minute. Learners may keep eyes open, look down, sit quietly, or skip the activity if they do not want to join.
checkQuestion: What is one thing you can do when your body feels stressed?
teacherNote: Keep the activity optional and calm. Do not ask learners to explain personal experiences. The goal is a short grounding routine, not counseling.

title: Asking for help
subject: Practical safety
description: Practice how to ask for help from a trusted adult without sharing private details in a group.
content: Children may need help with water, toilets, finding a teacher, feeling unwell, or understanding instructions. This lesson practices simple help-seeking words and safe choices. It does not ask children to describe private family situations.
goal: Ask a trusted adult for help using simple words, pointing, or a help card.
steps: Say together: I need help, please.
Name general trusted helpers in this learning space, such as teacher, volunteer, clinic worker, or community helper.
Practice three safe ways to ask: speaking, pointing, or showing a help card.
Practice choosing a safe place to stand: near the teacher, near the group, or another agreed safe place.
Remember: in a group lesson, you can ask for help without explaining private family details.
practice: Use gentle role-play cards: I need water, I need the toilet, I do not understand, I feel unwell, I cannot find my group. Learners choose a safe helper and practice asking with words, pointing, or a card.
checkQuestion: What is one safe way to ask for help if speaking feels hard?
teacherNote: Keep this protective and non-invasive. Do not ask children to identify personal risks, family problems, legal status, or conflict-related details. Review local referral pathways before using this in a real setting.

references.title: UNICEF: Learning Passport for crisis-affected learning

title: Learning review
subject: Review
description: Review numbers, reading, language, and safety with a short mixed activity.
content: Review what you learned today. Count five objects. Read one sentence. Say one helpful Thai or English word. Name one way to keep personal information private. Mark the lesson complete when you finish.
goal: Review one skill from numbers, reading, language, and safety.
steps: Count five safe objects near you.
Read one short sentence from a lesson.
Say one helpful Thai or English word.
Name one way to keep personal information private.
Choose one lesson you want to practice again.
practice: Learners can answer by speaking, pointing, drawing, writing, or showing objects. The teacher can turn this into a calm group review.
checkQuestion: Which activity felt easiest today, and which one do you want to practice again?
teacherNote: Use this as an end-of-session check. Learners can answer verbally, point, draw, or write depending on age and comfort.

title: Earthquake safety
subject: Emergency safety
description: Practice the widely recommended Drop, Cover, and Hold On action for earthquake shaking.
content: Earthquakes can happen with little warning. During shaking, the main action is Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Drop before shaking knocks you down. Cover your head and neck. Hold on until the shaking stops. After shaking, watch for broken glass, fallen objects, damaged areas, fire, or aftershocks.
goal: Practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On calmly, then review what to check after shaking stops.
steps: Drop down onto hands and knees so shaking does not knock you over.
Cover your head and neck. If a strong table is nearby, get under it. If not, cover with your arms.
Hold on to your shelter or position until the shaking stops.
Do not run outside during shaking. Do not use elevators.
After shaking stops, listen to a trusted adult and move carefully away from broken glass, fallen objects, or damaged areas.
practice: Do a calm 20-second drill. The teacher says, 'Earthquake.' Learners Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Then the teacher says, 'Shaking stopped.' Learners slowly stand, look for hazards, and point to a safe adult or meeting place.
checkQuestion: What are the three words to remember during earthquake shaking?
teacherNote: Practice this as a calm drill, not a frightening story. Adapt the lesson to the building type and local guidance. Ready.gov, ShakeOut, CDC, and UNICEF all recommend Drop, Cover, and Hold On and checking hazards after shaking.

references.title: ShakeOut: Drop, Cover, and Hold On
CDC: Stay safe during an earthquake

title: When danger is nearby
subject: Emergency safety
description: Practice simple civilian safety steps for loud danger, smoke, or explosions nearby.
content: If you hear danger nearby, stay with your group if it is safe. Move away from windows. Get low and protect your head and neck. Listen for trusted adult instructions. Do not run toward loud sounds, smoke, fire, damaged buildings, or crowds.
goal: Learn calm first actions when loud danger, smoke, or explosions are nearby.
steps: Pause and look for a trusted adult or group leader.
Move away from windows if it is safe to move.
Get low and protect your head and neck.
Stay with your group and listen for trusted adult instructions.
Do not run toward loud sounds, smoke, fire, damaged buildings, or crowds.
practice: Practice with a calm signal. The teacher says, 'Danger nearby.' Learners quietly crouch low, cover head and neck, and point to where a trusted adult would be.
checkQuestion: Should you run toward loud sounds or smoke?
teacherNote: Keep this general and non-tactical. Do not discuss weapons details or local military activity. Review the wording with trusted local protection or education workers before use.

title: Do not touch strange objects
subject: Emergency safety
description: Learn what to do if a child sees unknown metal, wires, shells, or dangerous debris.
content: If you see a strange object, do not touch it. Do not kick it, pick it up, throw it, or take it home. Move away calmly. Tell a trusted adult. Keep other children away if you can do that safely.
goal: Remember the safe rule for unknown objects: do not touch, move away, tell an adult.
steps: Stop before going closer to an unknown object.
Do not touch, kick, pick up, throw, or move the object.
Move away calmly using the same path if it is safe.
Tell a trusted adult what you saw and where you saw it.
Keep other children away only if you can do that safely.
practice: Use a harmless drawing of a strange object. Learners practice saying: Stop. Do not touch. Move away. Tell an adult.
checkQuestion: What should you do first if you see a strange object?
teacherNote: This lesson is for basic unexploded-object awareness. Use simple drawings or safe examples only. Do not show graphic images. Follow local mine-risk or explosive-risk education guidance where available.

title: Emergency bag basics
subject: Emergency safety
description: Learn simple items that families may prepare for emergencies if available.
content: An emergency bag can help if a family needs to move quickly. Useful items may include water, simple food, a flashlight, a whistle, a small cloth, basic medicine managed by an adult, and copies of important papers kept by an adult. Children should ask a trusted adult before packing or using medicine.
goal: Learn what an emergency bag is and why families may prepare one if they can.
steps: Ask a trusted adult where emergency items are kept.
Name simple useful items: water, simple food, flashlight, whistle, cloth, and adult-managed medicine.
Remember that important papers and medicine should be handled by adults.
Keep the bag in a place adults choose and children can remember.
Do not feel ashamed if your family does not have every item.
practice: Look at a picture or list of items. Learners choose three items that could help in an emergency and explain why.
checkQuestion: Who should manage medicine and important papers?
teacherNote: Present this as optional and realistic. Some families may not have these items. Avoid making learners feel ashamed if they cannot prepare a bag.
